title: A Testable Local Semantic Layer
text:
First draft · research as of 2026-10-01


Update, 2026-10-02: bounded native diagnostics now test evidence attribution and immediate repeatability. None of the tested interfaces passed its development gate; E09 records the counts and limits.


I started with a working job-search workflow. It reads alerts, extracts facts, checks history, applies rules and identifies what needs attention. Most of this is familiar Python backend work: parsing, lookups, exact comparisons and state transitions. The expensive part is interpreting language. Does an advertised role include managing people? Does a passage promise sponsorship, deny it, or say nothing? Does an answer supply the information requested and support what it claims?


I wanted those semantic operations to become cheap, local functions I could test. My first attempt compressed too much into one call: I gave Laya a workflow and asked it to choose drop or survive. It returned survive for all 300 historical roles. Perfect survivor recall was available from a constant function. I had obtained an allowed answer without transferring the workflow. That failure is the starting point of this book. Evidence E01


The question became more precise: can a small local model provide useful observations while Python retains policy, provenance, history and final authority? I call that proposed component “System 1.” This names an operational role, not a claim that a checkpoint reproduces human cognition. A generative worker or reviewer sometimes occupies the complementary “System 2” role. Neither name is an evaluation result.


I also want my explanations to earn their complexity. A cheap mental model can be enough to make the next engineering decision. When an observed failure exposes its limits, I can refine it. That deliberate simplification differs from accepting unsupported model predictions. Predictions require an error budget: which mistakes matter, what their consequences are, and how much useful recall or coverage the component must retain. “Never answer” and “always assert” can both fail the contract.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Observation stays separate from authority
    accDescr: Supplied text informs a bounded observation. Python checks its scope before policy chooses an action, while uncertainty can lead to review.
    Text["Supplied text"] --> Observe["Bounded observation"]
    Observe --> Check["Python checks scope"]
    Check --> Policy["Policy decides action"]
    Policy -. "uncertain" .-> Review["Request review"]
    Policy --> Record["Record result"]






Diagram: The proposed boundary lets a local model report an observation while Python checks scope and applies policy; uncertainty remains a reviewable state.


Eight branches developed around this question. The first is the workflow boundary: which judgments can be separated from policy? The second is the model interface: bounded options, extracted spans, claim support and passage relevance are different measurements. The third is zero-shot behavior: what changes when I alter wording, keys, distractors or evidence? These branches help me decide whether an apparent model failure is partly a poorly specified request.


The fourth branch defines answer quality. Requested-information coverage, evidence support, responsiveness and compliance can disagree, so I need separate judgments. The fifth asks where their reference labels come from. Independent model annotations improve the evidence available for debugging, but remain proxy references. Shared mistakes and disagreements survive a vote. Neither a fluent explanation nor model confidence supplies human ground truth.


The sixth branch puts annotation on my GPU. Spark finished more requests and ran faster when I disabled native thinking, but several judgments assessed its own output format instead of the target answer. The seventh branch preserves these failures as richer candidate supervision: source lineage, separate votes, missing labels, failure tags and proposed evidence spans. It also forces a distinction between evaluation masks, loss masks, attention masks and Laya’s option-position [MASK] tokens. The eighth sets the gate: what evidence would justify admitting any observation into the active harness?







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Research draws on several model disciplines
    accDescr: Natural language inference and evidence attribution, retrieval and relevance, selective prediction and abstention, robustness evaluation, proxy judge meta-evaluation, and future adaptation or distillation connect to distinct investigation questions. Tested work, design ideas, and future work are distinguished.
    NLI["NLI and evidence attribution: probed"] -->|"tests claim support"| Selective["Selective prediction and abstention: probed"]
    Retrieval["Retrieval and relevance: compared"] -->|"finds candidate passages"| NLI
    Robustness["Robustness evaluation: probed"] -->|"tests prompt sensitivity"| Selective
    Proxy["Proxy judge meta-evaluation: design"] -->|"checks reference quality"| NLI
    NLI -->|"could inform future"| Adaptation["Adaptation and distillation: future"]






Diagram: These conceptual links map borrowed tools to questions around one bounded semantic layer; they do not show a chronological pipeline or imply every technique is implemented.


These branches overlap. Better references can expose a prompt defect. A better prompt might remove the need for adaptation. A cheap local judge might generate candidate labels while creating a new adjudication burden. The chapter sequence makes this investigation readable; it does not imply a linear chronology from failed prompt to successful fine-tuning.


At this release, diagnostic runs, a wider native-interface comparison, prompt probes and a Spark pilot exist. No task fine-tuning has started. Synthetic optimizer and memory probes establish limited feasibility, not learned task performance. The expanded prompt study has now completed development and frozen-selection confirmation: results are mixed, with no broad prompt recipe established. The general annotation factory remains a parked specification. None of these experiments has replaced the production workflow.


This is the canonical authored book draft. Earlier articles and experiment notes remain research sources, rather than chapter copies to synchronize. The public evidence appendix gives short identifiers, denominators and limits; it deliberately does not expose private inputs or machine locations. Synthetic examples below illustrate the same distinctions without reproducing private correspondence.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Manuscript and public evidence appendix
    accDescr: Research sources inform the canonical draft. Its public evidence appendix reports denominators and limits while omitting private inputs.
    Research["Research sources"] --> Draft["Canonical book draft"]
    Draft --> Appendix["Public evidence appendix"]
    Appendix --> Limits["Denominators and limits"]
    Appendix --> Privacy["Private inputs omitted"]






Diagram: The appendix exposes enough evidence context to qualify claims without publishing private correspondence or machine locations.

title: 1. Start with a working workflow
text:
The tempting transfer was easy to describe. I already had a workflow that could explain why a role needed attention. A model accepted structured state and returned a typed choice. If I supplied enough of the workflow’s rules, perhaps that choice could become its final disposition. The interface looked like a function replacement. What I actually proposed was replacing several different functions, their stored history and their authority with one prediction.


Consider a fictional alert saying that a company wants an engineer to “lead the platform migration.” The phrase might describe technical responsibility. It does not necessarily mean the engineer will manage employees. Whether people management makes the role unsuitable is another question, owned by application policy. Whether I previously applied is a database lookup. Whether the alert is quoting an old vacancy is a provenance question. A single drop or survive answer hides which of those operations failed.


I learned this boundary through a blunt result. Laya retained all 300 historical roles. Reversing the options changed none of the decisions. Adding policy and candidate context also changed none. These controls ruled out those particular repairs on that fixture; they did not identify the internal cause. The useful conclusion was that this configuration had not reproduced the workflow. Calling the result high recall would conceal the absence of filtering. Evidence E01


I therefore reduced the model’s job to observations about supplied text. For the fictional alert, an observation might be people_management: not_stated, with the relevant source identifier. Python would decide what to do with an unresolved field: retain the role, request the full description or send it for review. This makes uncertainty actionable without turning it into permission. A sensor may fail; the application must know what that failure means.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Semantic observation within the workflow
    accDescr: The workflow parses an alert, obtains and validates an observation, applies policy and records an outcome. Unclear evidence can trigger review or a fuller source fetch through the application.
    Parse["Parse alert"] --> Observe["Observe text"]
    Observe --> Validate["Validate source"]
    Validate --> Policy["Apply policy"]
    Policy --> Record["Record outcome"]
    Policy -. "review or fetch" .-> Review["Application follow-up"]






Diagram: Semantic interpretation occupies one seam in the existing workflow; unresolved evidence follows an explicit application path.


The first useful design is deliberately ordinary. Parse the input. Preserve its identity. Ask one bounded semantic question. Validate the returned shape and provenance. Apply explicit policy to the observation. Record the result. I do not need a framework to express that sequence. I need an inspectable seam where I can replace the sensor, replay a request and compare its output against a reference without triggering an external action.


Some work should remain exact. Deduplication against a known identifier, salary arithmetic and recorded application history already have deterministic implementations. Asking a model to rediscover them creates an unnecessary failure surface. Language interpretation is different: an exact string search may miss a paraphrase or confuse technical leadership with management. The model earns consideration where that semantic ambiguity exists, not wherever the application happens to process text.


Even the observation boundary needs care. A quoted span can be genuinely present but refer to another person or another role. Substring validation proves that I did not fabricate the quote; it does not prove the quote supports the field. Conversely, absence from a short alert does not prove absence from the full description. I must carry the scope of the evidence through the system instead of letting a local prediction become a global fact.


This suggests a contract richer than a bare enum: the observation, evidence scope, source identity, model/configuration identity and validity status travel together. The contract does not need the model’s private reasoning. It needs enough observable information to reconstruct what was asked and reject unsupported use. If the source is incomplete, the backend should preserve that incompleteness.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Observable contract around a model result
    accDescr: An observation travels with its evidence scope, source identity and model configuration. Those fields support a validity check before use.
    Result["Observation"] --> Scope["Evidence scope"]
    Result --> Source["Source identity"]
    Result --> Config["Model and config"]
    Scope --> Gate["Use only if valid"]
    Source --> Gate
    Config --> Gate






Diagram: The contract supplies observable context for checking a result; it does not rely on private model reasoning.


My stopping rule also changes. I am no longer trying to make one model “understand the workflow.” I am trying to make one observation useful within a consequence-specific error budget. A field used only to prioritize manual review may tolerate different errors from a field that excludes a role. The threshold belongs to that use and must be declared before I select a favorable result.


The next question is what the instrument computes. A typed return value is helpful, but its meaning comes from a trained model and a particular request encoding. Chapter 2 opens that interface just far enough to explain why a valid answer can still be unsupported.

title: 2. What a decision model returns
text:
My cheapest useful mental model for Laya is a reader followed by an option scorer. The reader turns the request into contextual representations. The scorer compares the supplied choices and returns a distribution over them. It does not compose a chat response. This explains the appealing interface: the answer can stay inside an allowed set. It also explains the missing guarantee: nothing about membership in that set establishes that the chosen option follows from the evidence.


The tested stack uses ModernBERT-large, a bidirectional encoder, with additional decision machinery. The model card reports about 421 million parameters in total. “Bidirectional” means a token representation can incorporate surrounding request text; it does not mean the model executes every written instruction as a program. The options and criteria are inputs whose relationships to evidence must have been learned. ModernBERT paper, Laya checkpoint card


The versioned implementation places a [MASK] marker at each option position. After encoding and the extra decision layers, it gathers those marker representations, produces one scalar score per option and normalizes the scores with softmax. The marker is an address for the readout. It is not asking the language model to fill a missing word, and it is not an instruction to hide evidence. Laya implementation


Several questions about the same state become separate model rows that can share a batched forward call. The employment question does not consume the management question’s answer. Each is conditioned on the original state and its own question. That distinction matters if I want an answer to depend on an earlier result: the dependency must be implemented in the surrounding pipeline or in a changed architecture. Batching independent rows does not create deliberation between them. Batching implementation







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Option markers produce a bounded score distribution
    accDescr: The request includes option-position markers before encoding. The encoder and decision layers produce contextual representations from those positions, which are gathered into option scores and normalized with softmax.
    Request["Request with option markers"] --> Encoder["Encoder and decision layers"]
    Encoder --> Markers["Gather marker representations"]
    Markers --> Scores["One score per option"]
    Scores --> Softmax["Distribution over options"]






Diagram: The marker positions address option readouts; softmax ranks the supplied choices but does not establish that the choice is supported by evidence.


Request space is another part of the instrument. The inspected typed configuration has a 1,024-token total budget and a 256-token head budget; the versioned serializer also caps individual option descriptions. Longer instructions and longer options compete with evidence. A request can be structurally valid after shortening while losing the words that distinguish two options or establish a claim. I therefore need actual token and truncation diagnostics, not a character-count estimate. These are properties of that inspected configuration, not universal limits of every Laya release. Serialization source


The checkpoint is part of the contract too. The typed specialization was built around particular synthetic workflows. A schema that resembles those workflows does not make a new job-search task in-domain. “Typed” describes the interface and specialization; it does not mean universally competent at typed business questions. This is why I retain exact model and runtime identities alongside a result instead of reporting that “Laya” passed or failed in the abstract. Specialist model card


Confidence needs equally careful naming. In the inspected implementation, answer_confidence is the largest post-temperature option probability. For choice and score tasks, confidence measures concentration through normalized entropy. A concentrated distribution can be concentrated on an unsupported answer. Neither field automatically estimates correctness on my domain. Temperature fitting may improve calibration on suitable data, but it cannot restore missing evidence or create a semantic distinction the scores do not contain. Scoring implementation


I can now refine the backend analogy. This is a learned measurement service with a serializer, limited input budget, trained readout and domain-dependent score behavior. Type checking catches malformed use of the interface. Task evaluation determines whether the measurement is useful. Keeping those checks separate lets me diagnose a failure without pretending every wrong answer is a parsing bug or every clean response is reliable.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Interface checks and task evaluation answer different questions
    accDescr: The serializer fits a request to its input budget, then the model returns an output. Shape validation checks interface form; task evaluation checks whether the measurement is useful.
    Request["Request"] --> Serializer["Serialize within budget"]
    Serializer --> Model["Learned readout"]
    Model --> Shape["Validate output shape"]
    Shape --> Task["Evaluate task value"]






Diagram: A valid response shape establishes interface compliance; only task evaluation tests whether the measurement helps.


Chapter 3 uses this understanding to test the instrument: first with simple controls, then with sparse real evidence, and finally with narrower claim formulations.

title: 3. Test the instrument
text:
2026-10-02: Repeatability without reliability
After the all-survive result, I needed tests small enough to explain. A production-shaped benchmark can tell me that a system fails while leaving too many possible causes entangled. A literal positive, a literal denial and an absent fact ask a simpler question: can this instrument distinguish the relations my application depends on? These controls are not a substitute for realistic evaluation. They help decide what the realistic evaluation should measure.
The most consequential distinction was between denial and missing evidence. “The role does not include management” supports a negative observation. “The role maintains the data platform” may simply leave management unspecified. If both become no, the backend cannot tell an explicit exclusion from a sparse source. If missing evidence becomes yes, the sensor invents a fact. A third outcome such as not_stated is useful only if the model actually uses it appropriately.
The frozen sparse-alert check exposed this problem directly. Across 149 scorable head-level decisions inside 20 cards, 94 reference fields were not_stated. Laya returned not_stated correctly on none of those 94. Overall it matched 18 of 149 reference labels. These were diagnostic references, not human-certified truth, and multiple decisions share a card. I therefore treat the counts as strong evidence of a failure on this fixture, not 149 independent trials establishing a population error rate. Evidence E01
This result made an attractive shortcut untenable: I could not use schema validity as a proxy for evidence discipline. Every unsupported label could still be a legal enum. Nor could I report only recall on the fields the model asserted. A sensor that answers nearly everything may recover positive cases while flooding the application with invented facts. I need unsupported assertions beside useful supported and denied recall.
Diagram: The three relations keep absence of evidence distinct from evidence that denies a claim.
I next narrowed the task to whether supplied evidence establishes a claim. Natural-language inference, or NLI, gives a useful vocabulary: support, contradiction and unresolved relation. But I must inspect the actual model interface. A binary entailment score does not automatically distinguish contradiction from absence. Asking both a claim and its negation can help formulate a diagnostic, while also introducing a reconciliation rule whose behavior needs testing.
The Laya branch explored factual normalization, atomic heads, neutral option keys and bounded or dual-polarity claim formulations. Simple literal controls improved, but unrelated management and sponsorship evidence still produced errors. I stopped that tested branch from becoming a production route. The historical phrase “zero-shot exhausted” is too broad without this boundary: it means the configurations tried in that branch had not earned admission. It cannot settle every prompt, checkpoint or architecture. Evidence E01
A later, separate adapter experiment sharpened the trade-off. Forty configurations produced 1,440 decisions over 36 authored scenarios. No configuration passed its frozen gate, so its confirmation set remained unused. OpenJev’s bounded-QA configuration matched 29 of 36 references, but made unsupported assertions on 6 of 12 unresolved cases. Nano-Jev’s native groundedness route made none on those 12, while recovering only 3 of 9 support cases and 1 of 9 denial cases. Aggregate agreement concealed the operational difference. Evidence E02
I do not interpret zero observed unsupported assertions as zero risk. The sample is small, authored and task-specific. I also cannot reward a component merely for declining everything: native abstention, a valid semantic unresolved answer and a broken response are distinct events. The constant-unresolved baseline is useful precisely because it makes the no-information strategy visible.
Diagram: Separating malformed, abstaining and unresolved outcomes prevents schema failure or universal non-answering from counting as useful semantic coverage.
The experiment had reached a useful stopping point even without a winner. It showed why ordinary accuracy was the wrong selection rule and which failures needed a better instrument. Chapter 4 broadens the search by native task, while the prompt branch continues in parallel.
I next held the question small: three attributes, 24 authored development scenarios, six supported facts, six denials and twelve unresolved cases. Three unresolved cases contain conflicting evidence. Laya recovered 11/12 explicit facts; DeBERTa NLI and Kev recovered 12/12. Their unsupported assertions were nevertheless 9/12, 7/12 and 6/12. A frozen literal baseline recovered 9/12 facts with no unsupported assertions and 21/24 overall agreement. Its conservative quote/apostrophe guard limits what that comparison establishes. Evidence E09
Each canonical lane then received 108 transformed requests from those same 24 groups. Exact repetition changed zero labels out of 24 for every lane, while preserving ten Laya errors, seven NLI errors and six Kev errors. Repeatability here means the same immediate answer, including the same mistake; it establishes neither correctness nor long-term stability.
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Repeating an answer does not validate its evidence
    accDescr: A repeated request can return the same label, which may be correct or preserve an original error. Separate evidence changes probe whether the answer follows the right source and subject.
    Request["Repeat request"] --> Same["Same label"]
    Same --> Correct["Correct answer retained"]
    Same --> Error["Original error retained"]
    Edit["Change evidence or subject"] --> Scope["Test evidence attribution"]
Diagram: A stability check and an attribution check answer different questions.
DeBERTa reached the correct destination on all 24 complete counterfactual evidence edits, but only 17/24 pairs had both a correct source and destination. It also returned unresolved after all six support removals. Those are useful observations, not a minimal-negation causal test: complete evidence replacements change more than a single logical operator.
Attribution remained fragile. Subject changes produced errors on 6/6 NLI cases and 5/6 for each other lane. Distractors produced 16/24 NLI errors versus 3/24 for Kev. Removing support produced 4/6 Laya errors and 1/6 Kev errors. The architectures already perform useful language operations, but this fixture exposes failures in whose evidence counts and which evidence is irrelevant. It does not prove a bag-of-words mechanism or a capacity limit.

title: 3. Test the instrument
text:
Canonical results separate explicit fact recovery from unsupported assertions.














Robustness endpoint errors, with transformation-specific denominators and dependent scenario groups.

title: 4. Choose an interface before a model
text:
2026-10-02: Three native routes on the same local machine
A failed sensor made me look for alternatives, but “try another model” was too vague a plan. A passage ranker, an entity extractor and a claim verifier can all return numbers through a Python adapter. They are still measuring different things. I needed a map from the application’s question to the model’s native operation before I needed a leaderboard.
The implementations make these distinctions concrete. GLiNER2 offers schema-oriented extraction and classification; checkpoint capabilities still need checking. HHEM evaluates consistency with supplied evidence. Qwen’s reranker uses a decoder-based relevance readout, while Jina v3 ranks documents in a joint context. ColBERT uses token-level late interaction for retrieval. These are alternatives for different seams, not interchangeable truth meters.
The wider local study completed fourteen native lanes and 1,512 card records. Its confirmation portion contained 72 cards in twelve groups; this is separate from the adapter study whose confirmation never ran. The wider study used separate Astra and Gemini proxy references. Their confirmation status labels agreed on 58 of 72 cards, leaving fourteen disagreements. A candidate’s apparent quality therefore depended partly on which reference it was compared with. Evidence E03
The relevance lanes illustrate why I resist a unified ranking. MiniLM, Qwen and Jina ranked the small three-passage slates perfectly by nDCG@3 under both references, while token overlap was already strong. In a separate answer-annotation fixture, a contradicted answer received a Qwen relevance score of 0.99855. The answer was relevant to the question and wrong according to the evidence. No contradiction exists between those observations once I respect the score’s task. Evidence E03
Diagram: Claim support and passage relevance are separate measurements; the backend still owns the decision that uses either result.
The generative branch asks another question: which local worker is worth testing on a 12 GB GPU? The dated survey supplies a representative panel, not measured winners. Spark-X2.5-4B is the measured starting point. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 offers a nonthinking comparison. Phi-4-mini and Gemma 3 4B offer other model families. LFM2-2.6B and Qwen3.5-4B introduce different mixtures of recurrent or convolutional processing and attention. Their local task quality and memory behavior remain unmeasured here.
My initial memory model is simple: resident weights plus sequence state, working buffers and desktop headroom must fit. Four billion parameters at nominal four-bit packing require about 1.86 GiB for weights alone; at sixteen bits, about 7.45 GiB. Those are arithmetic lower bounds, not observed artifacts or total VRAM predictions. Quantization metadata, exceptional tensors, cache, concurrency and runtime allocation all matter. Advertised maximum context is especially poor evidence that my intended context fits.
Active parameters also differ from stored parameters. A mixture-of-experts model may activate only a fraction of its weights for each token while retaining many more weights. Qwen3-30B-A3B is therefore not a straightforward 12 GB fully resident candidate merely because its active count is small. Partial CPU offload is a separate latency and RAM trade-off. The historical OpenJev run used such offload; its timing is not an equal-hardware comparison with a small encoder.
Diagram: Parameter arithmetic offers a lower bound, while runtime allocation and the actual workload determine whether a local model fits.
The landscape leaves specific gaps: immutable pre-cutoff identities, exact licenses, label maps, selected quantizations, installed runtime support and measured allocation at the intended workload. I keep these as evidence tasks in the future-work ledger. More breadth becomes useful only when it tests a missing interface or a concrete cost hypothesis. Meanwhile, Chapter 5 asks what can improve without changing the model at all.
The next bounded study used cached Laya base English option scoring, DeBERTa NLI and Kev’s pointer route, all offline in FP32 on an RTX 3060. Kev used its frozen Qwen base with a native one-forward pointer readout; no generated chain of thought was involved. Fourteen runs completed 573 requests without invalid outputs or runtime failures. No weights were downloaded or trained, and no paid calls were made. Evidence E09
Runtime details constrain the comparison. Laya emitted a checkpoint temperature-clamping warning, retained in the evidence; its scores remain uncalibrated. Kev used slower reference kernels. Measured GPU fit establishes that these bounded workloads ran, not deployment calibration or a portable speed ranking. The next useful comparison is explicit entity/source conditioning and independent replication before introducing latent recurrence or training; a TRM head remains proposed, not implemented.

title: 5. Keep the prompt branch open
text:
I did not want dataset preparation to become an implicit decision to train. Another branch kept the checkpoint fixed and changed the request. This tests a different hypothesis: perhaps the model already has a useful distinction, but my interface fails to expose it. The branch can succeed on one task and fail on another. A blanket verdict about “prompt engineering” would erase that information.


The first controlled probe used six fictional cases, two checkpoints and eleven conditions: 132 decisions. Meaning-preserving changes included reordering, paraphrasing and adding irrelevant material. Evidence removal and decisive edits deliberately changed what the answer should be. These need opposite expectations: a good instrument should be stable under irrelevant changes and responsive to changes that alter support. Evidence E04


Both checkpoints were stable across the tested paraphrases and distractors, but each began with only four correct labels out of six. The persistent error was attribution. Evidence that Tomas owns a silver key does not deny that Mira owns a copper key. It leaves that claim unresolved. Both models answered denial, and explicit guidance did not fix it. Removing decisive evidence and making decisive edits worked on the simple controls. Stability and correctness had separated in a particularly useful way.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Prompt controls test stability and responsiveness
    accDescr: Meaning-preserving prompt changes should leave the answer stable. An edit to decisive evidence changes what the evidence supports and should change the answer.
    Prompt["Prompt condition"] --> Same["Meaning preserved"]
    Same --> Stable["Expect stable answer"]
    Edit["Decisive evidence edit"] --> Changed["Meaning changes"]
    Changed --> Responsive["Expect changed answer"]






Diagram: The probe separates stability under paraphrases and distractors from responsiveness to evidence changes.





Paired prompt controls show stable four-of-six baseline agreement and six-of-six agreement after the specified evidence-removal and decisive-edit transformations.




Figure: exploratory paired counts from six fixtures and four underlying claim families, not 132 independent examples. The transformations have different reference labels where meaning changes. This is a behavioral diagnostic, not a population accuracy estimate. See E04 for reference provenance and limitations.


A second probe used patterns from the public typed-decision training corpus to design fresh examples. Only TRAIN material was inspected; existing validation and test rows were not used. The current corpus revision was not independently linked to the exact cached training run. Its teacher labels were also not human truth. I used the corpus to form hypotheses about request structure, then evaluated newly authored inputs. Published corpus, Evidence E05


The 186 predictions comprised 156 main predictions and thirty tier-control predictions. Rewording an invoice reconciliation question moved base Laya from two correct cases out of four to four out of four. For typed Laya, meaningful invoice, order and delivery keys preserved four out of four; replacing them with generic field names reduced the result to two. Flattened prose retaining the semantic paths also achieved four. The evidence concerns semantic role information, not a demonstrated preference for JSON syntax.


Duplicate detection remained constant: base said yes to all four cases, typed said no to all four. Each matched two references but failed a different class. The published corpus’s negative-label imbalance was consistent with one possible explanation for typed behavior; it did not establish the cause. An exact comparator could solve these intentionally simple invoice cases. The experiment gave me a reason to preserve deterministic code, alongside a task-specific clue about wording.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Corpus patterns motivate fresh prompt probes
    accDescr: Training material patterns motivate a hypothesis, which is tested on newly authored scenarios. Development cases support selection while confirmation cases are reserved.
    Pattern["Training pattern"] --> Hypothesis["Prompt hypothesis"]
    Hypothesis --> Fresh["Fresh scenarios"]
    Fresh --> Development["Development selection"]
    Development --> Confirmation["Reserved confirmation"]






Diagram: Corpus inspection shaped a hypothesis, while fresh development and reserved confirmation cases provide separate checks.


These fixtures were tiny and included near-replicates. The expanded study used fifty scenarios per task: invoice reconciliation, duplicate detection and evidence support. Ninety development cases received four fixed conditions across both checkpoints, producing 720 predictions. Selection was frozen before sixty confirmation cases received baseline and the selected condition, producing 180 predictions. References were independently model-reviewed synthetic labels. Confirmation contains fresh cases within ten shared mechanism patterns per task, not unseen mechanism families. Evidence E06


Development exposed useful contrasts without establishing a general recipe. Operational wording moved base invoice matching from 15/30 to 21/30: eight repairs and two regressions. The two regressions exceeded the registered gate, so that variant was not selected or tested in confirmation. Typed invoice matching instead fell from 17/30 to 15/30 under the same intervention. Base prose repaired five invoice cases and broke five, leaving 15/30 unchanged. An average alone would have hidden those opposing changes.

The one confirmation repair was an exact invoice-ID/vendor pair in a three-entry history. Typed exact-pair recall improved only from 1/10 to 2/10; the descriptive clustered interval for the overall paired gain was zero to fifteen percentage points. Base evidence prose turned an unknown prerequisite into an unsupported conclusion: “If the switch is enabled, the sensor is active” does not establish activity when the switch state is unknown. The development gains for base duplicate and evidence prose did not recur as confirmation improvements.


The concrete contrasts give me testing heuristics. Name the intended operation, preserve semantic roles, and include near matches, wrong subjects, missing attributes and conflicting sources as controls. Count repairs, regressions and wrong-to-wrong flips separately. These are ways to diagnose prompts, not a winning prompt recipe. In development, both checkpoints handled every direct support, denial and negation example, but failed every missing-attribute and equal-authority conflict example. Familiar language cues may be easier to access than relational bookkeeping; this is a behavioral hypothesis, not an attention-level finding. Exact equality and arithmetic still favor deterministic comparators.


The discipline matters more than a favorable ending. Once I inspect an error and design a repair, that example becomes development evidence. Its paraphrases must stay in the same split. A larger count of related variants does not manufacture independent confirmation. These questions lead directly to the next branch: what should the reference answer mean?

title: 6. Separate the dimensions of an answer
text:
“Is this a good answer?” sounds like one question until I try to debug a negative label. Consider this synthetic request: “Give the workshop date and price in one sentence.” The supplied evidence says that it runs on Tuesday and costs twenty euros. An answer saying “The workshop runs on Tuesday” is supported but incomplete. An answer supplying Tuesday and thirty euros covers the requested fields while inventing the price. A relevance score alone cannot distinguish the two failures.


I use four dimensions because each changes a different decision about repair. Coverage asks which requested information units are addressed. Evidence support asks whether the assertions actually made have support. Responsiveness asks whether the answer engages the request and its intended referent. Compliance asks whether the target answer follows constraints such as format. An answer may fail several at once, but that does not make them synonyms.


The target matters. If the request demands one sentence, compliance concerns the workshop answer. The judge may itself be required to return JSON containing several fields. Whether that JSON is valid is an operational validation question, separate from whether the workshop answer followed its instruction. I initially treated this distinction as obvious. The local-judge experiment would show why obvious distinctions still need to be encoded and tested.


My own expected labels were enough to begin debugging, but they could also encode my mistakes. I therefore gathered separate model annotations with candidate predictions and other votes hidden on the first pass. Astra and Gemini supplied proxy references, retained separately. Independent annotation passes reduce one route of contamination; they do not make the annotators independent truth sources or eliminate shared biases. Evidence E03


Disagreement is useful data. If one judge interprets a phrase as an explicit denial and another treats it as unresolved, I need to inspect the rubric, evidence scope and possible ambiguity. Collapsing the two votes into a majority label would discard that uncertainty. On the wider study’s confirmation statuses, fourteen of 72 cards had different Astra and Gemini labels. Candidate agreement can shift materially with the chosen reference; that shift belongs in the report.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
accTitle: Four answer dimensions
accDescr: The same candidate answer is evaluated separately for coverage, evidence support, responsiveness, and compliance.
    A["Candidate answer"] --> B["Requested information covered?"]
    A --> C["Assertions supported?"]
    A --> D["Right request and referent?"]
    A --> E["Target follows constraints?"]






Diagram: The four dimensions branch from one answer because each diagnoses a different kind of repair.


A reference record needs its own identity: judge, rubric version, source inputs, validity checks and any later adjudication. If a revised rubric changes what “coverage” means, I must not pool the new labels with old labels as though the instrument stayed fixed. A human-adjudicated subset would help assess the proxies, but no such gold standard exists in the completed studies described here. Agreement remains agreement with a named reference.


This also separates three quantities that are easily conflated. A model’s reported confidence describes its own scoring behavior. Agreement describes consistency between outputs. Calibration compares predictions with outcomes under a specified reference and distribution. None can silently replace the others. Category-specific trust would require sufficiently reliable adjudicated cases, separate calibration data and an untouched evaluation, not a confident vote attached to a small fixture.


The practical payoff is a more useful correction. For the incomplete workshop answer, I can preserve supported assertions and request the missing price. For the invented-price answer, I must correct the evidence failure. A binary bad label loses this distinction and may teach a future model to confuse omission with fabrication. The richer record therefore improves both present diagnosis and the quality of possible future supervision.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
accTitle: Proxy votes and reference limits
accDescr: Astra and Gemini provide separate votes for a candidate output; retaining both exposes disagreement, while neither vote is human-adjudicated gold.
    A["Candidate output"] --> B["Astra vote"]
    A --> C["Gemini vote"]
    B --> D["Keep votes separate"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["No human gold yet"]






Diagram: Separate proxy votes preserve disagreement and keep the reference limitation visible.


Reference quality also creates a cost question. If every routine annotation requires an expensive remote judge and subsequent review, local inference may help. Chapter 7 tests that possibility on the actual GPU, keeping operational success separate from semantic agreement.
crumbs: 7  6. Separate the dimensions of an answer

title: 7. Put the annotator on my GPU
text:
The local-judge question was economic and empirical: could Spark supply useful annotations while reducing routine frontier-model calls? Loading weights would answer only a preliminary question. I needed complete outputs, valid provenance and acceptable judgments, and I needed to count the work required to review failures. Local inference is not automatically free or cheaper end to end.


The pilot used the official Spark-X2.5-4B Q8_0 artifact through an isolated llama.cpp runtime on an RTX 3060. The configuration allowed one request at a time, a 4,096-token context and a 2,048-token completion cap. Observed GPU allocation was around 4.5 GiB; polling did not establish a continuous peak. This was a generative annotation route, not Spark’s separate bounded-option harness. Official Spark repository, Evidence E07


Native thinking produced one accepted output from twelve attempts. Eleven reached the completion limit without final labels. Those failures consumed time but did not provide eleven semantic decisions to score. The rendered prompts plus completions remained below the context limit, so enlarging context alone would not explain or repair the observed output-budget failure.


Disabling thinking through the native template preserved the task and rubric. Seven of twelve outputs then passed strict validation. The other five finished with valid JSON but invalid evidence identifiers. Median latency fell from 34.31 seconds to 3.85 seconds. That is a useful operational improvement on these requests. It does not show semantic superiority because the accepted subsets differ, and repaired citations were not admitted as valid benchmark outputs.





Spark operational comparison: one versus seven accepted outputs from twelve attempts per mode, with median latency falling from 34.31 to 3.85 seconds.




Figure: twelve attempts per mode on the same twelve cards, representing six paired groups. Accepted-output coverage and latency describe this pilot. Budget-exhausted and citation-invalid outputs remain separate failures; these bars do not measure human accuracy.


Among the seven accepted nonthinking outputs, coverage agreed with both proxies on all seven and evidence support on five. Compliance agreed on one against Astra and none against Gemini; responsiveness agreed on five and six respectively. The denominator seven is appropriate for that conditional semantic comparison. The denominator twelve remains necessary for pipeline success and cost. Selecting valid outputs does not make them representative of the failures excluded.





Conditional agreement for four answer dimensions among the seven accepted nonthinking outputs, with Astra and Gemini references shown separately.




Figure: proxy agreement on the selected valid seven of twelve outputs, not accuracy on twelve attempts. Reference disagreement remains visible. With only six underlying paired groups, these descriptive counts cannot establish deployment reliability.


Inspection of all 24 outputs across the two modes exposed a narrower hypothesis than “the model is too small.” Eight of the twelve nonthinking compliance rationales assessed the judge’s own annotation format instead of the target answer. Five were accepted outputs; three were citation-invalid and inspected only for diagnosis. Other judgments confused omitted requested information with unsupported assertions. I can describe these observable errors without claiming to know their internal mechanism.


The next inexpensive tests would isolate the target answer, ask atomic dimension questions and separate bounded labels from optional citations. Structured decoding might prevent some shape errors, but cannot establish that the judgment concerns the right text. None of these semantic interventions has been demonstrated here. The larger 108-card Spark job benchmark did not run, and the owned server was stopped after preserving the pilot evidence.


Spark made the cost question more concrete. Faster completion can reduce one expense while invalid provenance and mistaken targets increase review. The useful comparison is cost per sufficiently reliable, accepted annotation, with failed calls included. Chapter 8 explains why preserving those failures creates a better candidate corpus than keeping only the successful labels.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
accTitle: Spark pilot outcomes by mode
accDescr: Twelve attempts in each mode yielded one accepted thinking output with eleven budget failures, and seven accepted nonthinking outputs with five citation-invalid outputs.
    A["Same task and rubric"] --> B["Thinking"]
    B --> C["1 accepted of 12"]
    B --> D["11 budget failures"]
    A --> E["Nonthinking"]
    E --> F["7 accepted of 12"]
    E --> G["5 citation-invalid"]






Diagram: This records pipeline outcomes by mode; semantic agreement was computed only on the selected valid nonthinking outputs.
crumbs: 8  7. Put the annotator on my GPU

title: 8. Build examples worth learning from
text:
The experiments are producing a corpus, but “dataset” can imply more readiness than I have earned. I currently have candidate annotations, source records and failure diagnoses. I do not have a certified training set. The general annotation factory remains a specification; small scripts that preserve its rules do not amount to a deployed factory.


A useful example preserves the question, supplied evidence, source identifiers, scenario group, rubric version, each reference vote, candidate prediction and validation result. It can add proposed evidence spans, counterfactual relationships and a failure tag. For the key-ownership example, a tag such as wrong_subject records a behavioral diagnosis. It does not identify a neuron, prove an attention defect or prescribe the training method that will repair it.


For the workshop example, rich supervision keeps supported assertions separate from missing requested information. One dimension might be usable while another remains disputed. A single positive/negative label would force me to lose that distinction or invent certainty. Separate votes and lineage let me revisit the record after improving the rubric, without rewriting history to make the old labels look cleaner.


Four different meanings of “mask” now matter. They affect different stages and must never be inferred from one another:










Mask
Job
What it does not imply




Annotation/evaluation eligibility mask
Select fields with a usable reference for a particular comparison
Invalid attempts disappear from operational counts


Future loss mask
Select supervised targets that contribute to an objective
Every available vote is trustworthy supervision


Attention mask or evidence-routing supervision
Restrict access to input positions or train a specified evidence relationship
A proposed evidence span already implements a training intervention


Laya option [MASK] marker
Identify the contextual position read by the option scorer
An evidence restriction or missing target










%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
accTitle: Four distinct mask jobs
accDescr: Evaluation eligibility selects comparison fields; a future loss mask selects supervised targets; an attention mask restricts input access; evidence-routing supervision instead trains a specified evidence relationship; and Laya MASK marks the option-scoring position.
    A["Distinct mask jobs"] --> B["Eval selects fields"]
    A --> C["Loss selects targets"]
    A --> D["Attention limits input"]
    A --> E["Laya MASK marks option"]






Diagram: The four mechanisms have different jobs, so one mask never implies the behavior of another.


An unresolved reference is often a valid target, not a missing annotation. A malformed judge output is different. In evaluation, I can exclude that judge’s unusable field from a semantic denominator while still counting its failed attempt. In future training, I might withhold a disputed field, adjudicate it or use a justified soft target. Disagreement does not automatically define a probability distribution suitable for a loss.


Evidence tags need similar restraint. Restricting attention to a highlighted span might remove a negation, a pronoun antecedent or a conflicting sentence. An auxiliary evidence objective is different from a hard attention restriction. High attention on a token does not by itself demonstrate causal use. If teacher annotations appear only during training, the student must also be trained and evaluated for its intended annotation-free deployment path; otherwise I have changed the input contract.


Lineage determines the split. Original scenarios, paraphrases, counterfactuals, head rows and derived annotation cards belong together before flattening. Related employer, requisition or conversation records need the same care where applicable. Once I mine a failure to design a prompt or training target, its relatives cannot serve as fresh confirmation of that repair. More rows do not mean more independent evidence.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
accTitle: Group related records before splitting
accDescr: An original scenario and its paraphrases, counterfactuals, head rows, and derived annotation cards stay in one lineage group, which is assigned wholly to one split.
    A["Original scenario"] --> B["Related variants and cards"]
    B --> C["One lineage group"]
    C --> D["One split only"]






Diagram: Grouping relatives before assigning splits prevents mined variants from masquerading as fresh confirmation.


The practical artifact is a revisable evidence record, not a verdict dump. It supports error analysis today and leaves training choices explicit for later. That brings me to Chapter 9: which intervention would answer a diagnosed question, and what would make running it justified?
crumbs: 9  8. Build examples worth learning from

title: 9. When training would be justified
text:
No task fine-tuning has started. That status is compatible with serious training research: I can inspect an upstream recipe, measure optimizer memory and design candidate supervision without having trained a useful task model. Keeping those activities separate prevents a feasibility result from becoming a performance claim.


My first training question would be whether the existing representations already contain a distinction that a new head can learn. Head-only adaptation freezes the reader and changes the decision boundary. A negative result would be informative only under a competent training setup and adequate supervision; it would not automatically prove the representation contains no useful signal. A positive result would still need grouped confirmation and comparison with the unchanged checkpoint.


LoRA offers a different hypothesis: modest changes to selected projections may adapt the reader without updating every weight. It is a choice about trainable parameters, not a guarantee of better generalization or lower harmful-error risk. Full-parameter training permits broader changes at a greater optimization and memory cost. The comparison should follow the diagnosed error and resource budget, rather than treating head-only, LoRA and full training as a mandatory progression. Official LoRA guide


I am particularly interested in attention-projection adaptation. Query/key changes affect routing; including value/output projections also changes what information is transported and combined. “Attention-only” is therefore insufficient specification. I would record the exact layers and projections, freeze everything else deliberately and compare against a head-only baseline. Attention maps are input-dependent activations, not persistent parameters that can simply be edited into a reusable policy.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
accTitle: Possible training routes
accDescr: A diagnosed error can motivate alternative interventions: head-only adaptation changes the decision boundary, LoRA changes selected projections, and full training changes all weights.
    A["Diagnosed error"] --> B["Head only: new boundary"]
    A --> C["LoRA: selected projections"]
    A --> D["Full: all weights"]






Diagram: These are alternative hypotheses to match to an error and resource budget, not a demonstrated sequence or result.


The inspected upstream Laya notebook uses full-parameter training with separate encoder and head learning rates, checkpointing and later calibration work. It is an explanatory reference, not a verified reconstruction of every released checkpoint’s training history. Nor does its use of two GPUs mean their memory becomes one shared pool under ordinary distributed data parallelism. Local feasibility needs a local measurement. Upstream notebook


A synthetic steady-state optimizer probe did complete on the 12 GB GPU. With 1,024-token rows, accumulation over four micro-batches, checkpointing, FP32 weights/gradients/Adam state and FP16 autocast with loss scaling, the eight-row micro-batch peaked at 8.2186 GiB allocated and 8.9062 GiB reserved. It completed a second optimizer update so persistent optimizer state was included. This made local full-parameter experimentation plausible. Evidence E08


The probe did not include the complete upstream auxiliary exploration, all data-pipeline variation, evaluation passes or checkpoint writes. Its synthetic shape was not a real task-learning run. A short end-to-end smoke test would still be necessary before a longer experiment, with exact trainable parameters, effective batch size, warmup, gradient clipping, loss scaling, loss logging and versioned checkpoints recorded. Code and configuration must be snapshotted before each run.


Training also needs a target worth learning. Repeated errors, sufficiently trustworthy supervision, grouped splits and a suitable baseline must precede the optimizer. Calibration data must remain separate from training and final evaluation. Any teacher evidence supplied only during training must be absent from the deployment evaluation unless the deployed system truly includes that teacher. Otherwise the experiment answers the wrong engineering question.







%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
accTitle: Dependencies before a longer run
accDescr: Before a longer task run, a persistent error needs trustworthy supervision, grouped splits, and a suitable baseline; those prerequisites lead to a short end-to-end smoke test first.
    A["Persistent error"] --> B["Trustworthy supervision"]
    A --> C["Grouped splits"]
    A --> D["Suitable baseline"]
    B --> E["Short smoke test"]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F["Longer task run"]






Diagram: These are prerequisites for a proposed experiment; no task-training run has started.


The objective is not simply higher agreement. It is fewer harmful accepted assertions at useful coverage, with uncertainty and cost visible. If a simpler prompt or deterministic check meets that contract, training may be unnecessary. Chapter 10 makes the acceptance decision explicit.
crumbs: 10  9. When training would be justified

title: 10. Earn a place in the harness
text:
2026-10-02: A development gate that stayed closed
The investigation has not produced a production replacement. It has produced something more specific than a vague failure: a tested boundary, preserved negative results, candidate reference annotations and a set of smaller questions. I can now say what evidence would change my decision. That is a useful engineering outcome even while the active workflow remains unchanged.
I would begin with the consuming operation. What happens when this observation is wrong? Which errors are harmful, and how much useful recall or coverage makes the component worth running? A sensor used to order a review queue has a different contract from one used to discard an opportunity. A single global accuracy threshold would blur those consequences. The numeric error budget remains a future policy decision, not a number to invent after seeing a promising model.
Then I would freeze the task, inputs, source identities, rubric, native request, output validation and baselines. Deterministic checks and constant/deferral strategies deserve explicit comparison. Candidate selection and threshold tuning belong on development groups. Only after selection is locked should untouched confirmation groups assess the proposed route. If the uncertainty remains too wide, the honest outcome is insufficient evidence, not an extrapolated guarantee.
Diagram: This dependency order prevents development choices from using confirmation evidence; no threshold is supplied here.
Risk and coverage should appear together. Selective risk asks how often accepted judgments are wrong under the specified reference. Useful coverage asks how much work those accepted judgments accomplish. A threshold can reduce the first by abandoning the second. I also need per-category unsupported assertions and polarity recall, because an aggregate curve can hide a disastrous subgroup. Invalid outputs, abstentions and valid unresolved labels remain distinct throughout.
Proxy references set a limit on the claim. Their agreement can guide development and expose clear failures, but a production gate needs independently adjudicated evidence appropriate to the consequences. Calibration must be assessed on the target distribution. Related scenarios require grouped uncertainty; repeated prompt variants cannot make confidence intervals artificially narrow. Even observing no harmful errors leaves a nonzero upper risk bound.
Cost is equally task-specific. I would include loading, prefill, output tokens, failed requests, latency tails, memory and review time. A local model that is faster per call can still be more expensive per useful annotation. Hardware comparisons must preserve quantization, offload, context and concurrency. The Spark pilot provides an operational observation, while the wider landscape supplies hypotheses awaiting measurement.
The next work has a dependency order without requiring a linear research story. Resolve candidate identities and native constraints. Define the consuming error budget. Improve reference quality. Test the smallest diagnosed prompt or task-boundary hypothesis. Revisit adaptation only if a persistent error and usable supervision justify it. The future-work ledger records these gaps as actual evidence tasks; they are not unfinished chapter prose or promises that an experiment will succeed.
Any eventual admission should be narrow and reversible. The model supplies an observation; Python checks evidence scope, policy and authority before taking action. A replacement sensor must be replayable and removable. Changing a checkpoint, prompt, rubric or source distribution can invalidate the evidence that supported admission, so those changes require a proportionate reevaluation rather than inheriting permanent trust.
Diagram: The model provides evidence for a decision; the application owns the deterministic authority gate.
I began by trying to transfer a workflow into one typed choice. I now have a more demanding and more testable goal: make one semantic operation cheap enough, useful enough and bounded enough for a particular place in the application. The simplest component that meets that contract is enough. When it fails, the next refinement should answer the failure I measured.
The bounded study supplied a concrete experimental gate without settling production policy. Kev’s question interface recovered 5/6 supported facts and 6/6 denials, and asserted on none of the three conflicts. It still asserted on 3/12 unresolved cases, exceeding the frozen allowance of at most 1/12. No tested interface qualified; the conditional 324-request extension remained unexecuted. None has yet earned a larger independent evaluation. Evidence E09
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: The development gate prevents an unearned extension
    accDescr: Tested native interfaces fail the frozen development eligibility gate, so the conditional extension does not run. Diagnosed attribution failures instead inform a proposed new development protocol.
    Interfaces["Native interfaces tested"] --> Gate["Frozen development gate"]
    Gate --> Failed["No eligible interface"]
    Failed --> Stopped["Conditional extension not run"]
    Failed --> Proposed["Propose attribution controls"]
Diagram: A failed gate changes the next research question; it does not silently relax the admission rule.
All new cases are development material built around known failure types and templates. Independently reviewed model-origin labels remain provisional. Grouped descriptive uncertainty cannot turn them into an IID sample, a statistically winning model or proof of pretraining freshness. Job search is the first testbed for a general semantic harness; Python’s policy, provenance and final authority remain unchanged, and no annotation factory has been implemented.

This reporting distinction never overrides a prediction using the reference label. Kev bounded QA recovered 5/6 support and 6/6 denial, with 3/12 unresolved assertions and zero conflict assertions; no interface passed the frozen gate, and the conditional 324-request extension did not run.
Repeated labels disagreed on 0/24 for each canonical lane, retaining 10/7/6 endpoint errors for Laya/NLI/Kev. NLI counterfactual destinations were correct on 24/24, but both source and destination were correct on 17/24. Support removal errors were 4/6, 0/6, 1/6; subject-change errors 5/6, 6/6, 5/6 respectively. NLI distractor errors were 16/24; Kev’s were 3/24. These dependent development diagnostics do not establish production reliability, minimal-negation causality, a capacity limit or a statistically superior model.

title: Evidence and future-work ledger
text:
Future work


These IDs track missing evidence, not incomplete prose. Proposed experiments require their own bounded protocol and resources; this book does not report them as executed.
